*   According to the US CDC ArboNET provisional data (current as of 02 Dec 2025), the United States has reported 1981 total West Nile virus (WNV) disease cases across 46 states, including 1359 neuroinvasive disease cases.
*   The exact national total of WNV deaths in the US for 2025 has not yet been formally finalized or published by the US CDC.
*   States reporting the highest numbers of cases in 2025 include Colorado (284), Illinois (137), Texas (115), and Minnesota (112).
*   In comparison, 1791 cases, including 1335 neuroinvasive cases and164 deaths, were reported in the US in 2024.
*   The 2025 WNV season in the US is coming to an end; however, due to reporting delays, additional cases may still be recorded.

**Epidemiological analysis and public health impact**

*   In the United States, the 2025 West Nile virus season was marked by a prolonged period of risk, consistent with climate-driven lengthening of the mosquito season.
*   Entomologic and avian surveillance data from multiple jurisdictions continued to demonstrate enzootic amplification in birds and _Culex_ mosquitoes as a precursor to human disease, reinforcing the importance of integrated vector management and early-season indicators.
*   In the absence of licensed human vaccines or specific antivirals, the 2025 season highlighted the centrality of prevention—personal bite avoidance, targeted vector control, and blood/transplant safety measures—as well as the need to adapt WNV preparedness to a progressively longer and more intense transmission season.
*   The geographic distribution across 46 states demonstrates the virus's endemic establishment throughout the contiguous United States, with transmission occurring in both historically high-burden regions (Southwest, Mississippi Delta, Great Plains, Rocky Mountain areas) and states with more variable case counts. This widespread distribution increases the likelihood that healthcare providers will encounter cases even in areas without consistent annual transmission, potentially leading to delayed diagnosis and treatment.
*   The US CDC has been investigating multiple clusters potentially linked to blood transfusions, organ transplants, and dialysis procedures, with 15 transplant-associated clusters documented between 2002 and 2024.
*   WNV has been seen in organ transplant recipients. “We are aware of 15 transplant clusters associated with West Nile during 2002 to 2024,” reported[Capt. Carolyn Gould, MD, MSCR, US CDC](https://www.ama-assn.org/public-health/infectious-diseases/west-nile-virus-deaths-32-2025). Infections in these patients are associated with higher morbidity and mortality.Most of the organ donors involved in these clusters were not screened for WNV, she said, adding that screening could prevent many of these cases.

**Comparative analysis and future outlook**

*   S ince its detection in the US in 1999, West Nile virus has become the most commonly reported arboviral disease in the contiguous United States.
*   Among those with neuroinvasive disease, one in 10 will die, said AMA (American Medical Association) infectious-diseases director[Erica Kaufman West, MD](https://find-doctor.ama-assn.org/doctor/erica-elizabeth-kaufman-md/21850487).
*   While the 2025 season has not reached the levels seen in 2002 (4156 cases) or during the 2021 Arizona outbreak (1600+ cases in a single state), the ongoing burden of severe disease and deaths warrants continued surveillance.
*   Transplant-associated and transfusion-related clusters represent a rare but evolving transmission pathway that bypasses traditional mosquito-vector control measures. These iatrogenic transmission routes can result in particularly severe outcomes, as immunosuppressed transplant recipients experience higher morbidity and mortality. The fact that most organ donors involved in documented clusters were not screened for WNV indicates a gap in transplant safety protocols that could be addressed through enhanced donor screening during peak transmission seasons.
*   Although WNV infection is typically seasonal, with most cases occurring in summer and early fall, transfusion- or transplant-associated WNV disease can present beyond that period.

**Pathogen characteristics**

*   West Nile virus is a flavivirus primarily transmitted through bites from infected _Culex_ species mosquitoes, with transmission typically occurring during summer and fall months (June through October) when mosquito populations peak. The virus can also be transmitted through infected blood products, transplanted organs, and rarely from mother to child during pregnancy, delivery, or breastfeeding. The incubation period ranges from 2 to 14 days, with most symptomatic cases developing between 2 and 6 days after infection.
*   Approximately 80% of WNV infections are asymptomatic, while 20% of infected individuals develop West Nile fever, characterized by the sudden onset of fever, headache, body aches, joint pains, vomiting, diarrhea, or rash. About 1% of infections progress to neuroinvasive disease, including encephalitis, meningitis, or acute flaccid myelitis, with case fatality rates of 10% to 15% among those with neurological complications. The virus has become endemic throughout the contiguous United States since its introduction in 1999, with ongoing potential for seasonal epidemic transmission at local, regional, or national levels.
*   No specific antiviral treatments or vaccines are currently available for WNV disease in humans, making management entirely supportive. Treatment focuses on symptom management, hydration, and intensive care for patients with neurological complications. Prevention remains the primary strategy, including personal protective measures (mosquito repellent, long-sleeved clothing, avoiding outdoor activities during peak mosquito hours), environmental control (eliminating standing water, using larvicides and adulticides), and screening of blood products and organ donors during transmission seasons to prevent iatrogenic transmission.

### **2026 WNV+ Dead Birds**

Residents [report dead birds](http://westnile.ca.gov/report_wnv.php) through the California Department of Public Health (CDPH) Dead Bird Surveillance program.  After a bird is reported, the District collects it and tests it for West Nile virus if it meets the established testing criteria. Positive dead birds also provide insight to West Nile virus activity.

**So far in 2026, a total of 8 birds in Newark and Fremont have tested positive for West Nile virus in Alameda County.**

### **West Nile Virus Activity (WNV+) in Alameda County**

Visit the full [VectorSurv site](https://maps.vectorsurv.org/arbo) to learn more about mosquito and disease activity throughout California.

## What does the Alameda County Mosquito Abatement District do after a dead bird and/or a mosquito pool tests positive for West Nile virus?

When a dead bird or mosquito pool tests positive for West Nile virus (WNV), District staff respond by:

* Deploying additional mosquito monitoring traps in the area
* Inspecting for and eliminating or treating standing water sources, such as storm drains, ponds, and unmaintained swimming pools, using larvicides when appropriate
* Expanding community outreach and public education efforts
* Implementing targeted mosquito control treatments as needed

# First Illinois West Nile Virus Death of 2024 is Reported by IDPH in Lake County

News – Tuesday, August 27, 2024

[Email](mailto:?subject=I%20thought%20you%20might%20find%20this%20interesting&body=https://dph.illinois.gov/resource-center/news/2024/august/first-illinois-west-nile-virus-death-of-2024-is-reported-by-idph.html "Share by Email")

{ "@context": "http://schema.org", "@type": "NewsArticle", "url": "", "datePublished": "2024-08-27T00:00:00.000Z", "headline": "", "mainEntityOfPage": "" }

**CHICAGO** – The Illinois Department of Public Health (IDPH) announced the first 2024 death of an Illinois resident with West Nile virus (WNV).  The individual, who was in their 80’s and lived in Lake County, had an onset of symptoms of WNV in mid-August and died soon after. IDPH is also reporting nine non-fatal cases of WNV confirmed to date this year.

“Sadly, Illinois is reporting our first death of the year attributed to West Nile virus,” said IDPH Director Dr. Sameer Vohra. “This death – and the six that occurred last year in Illinois - are a stark reminder that West Nile virus poses a serious risk, especially to older people and those with weakened immune systems. This is why while warm weather continues and mosquitoes are breeding, we should all take steps to ‘Fight the Bite.’ Please protect yourself and your loved ones by reducing exposures, repelling insects with clothing and repellents, and reporting locations at high risk for producing mosquitoes.”

Of the nine other human cases in 2024 to date, the majority were reported from Cook County, with others in in DuPage, Will, Winnebago and Tazewell counties.

The first WNV-related death in Illinois in 2023 also had an onset of symptoms in August. There were six deaths from WNV confirmed in the state in 2023 and an additional 119 non-fatal cases reported (although human cases are underreported).  The youngest person to report a case of West Nile virus in Illinois last year was 33 years old, while the median age of human cases was 67.

West Nile virus is transmitted through the bite of a *Culex* mosquito, commonly called a typical mosquito, which has picked up the virus by feeding on an infected bird. Common symptoms of WNV include fever, nausea, headache and muscle aches. Symptoms may last from a few days to a few weeks. Four out of five people infected with West Nile virus will not show any symptoms. However, in rare cases, severe illness can occur, including brain infections such as meningitis or encephalitis and paralysis or even death. People older than 50 and immunocompromised individuals are at higher risk for severe illness from West Nile virus.

There is no specific treatment for WNV nor is there a vaccine at present, therefore it is critically important that people minimize their risk of being infected by it.

IDPH encourages the public to *Fight the Bite* and take steps to prevent WNV by practicing the three “R’s” – reduce, repel, and report:

* **REDUCE**- make sure doors and windows have tight-fitting screens.  Repair or replace screens that have tears or other openings.  Try to keep doors and windows shut. Eliminate, or refresh each week, all sources of standing water where mosquitoes can breed, including water in bird baths, ponds, flowerpots, wading pools, old tires, and any other containers.
* **REPEL** - when outdoors, wear shoes and socks, long pants and a light-colored, long-sleeved shirt, and apply an EPA-registered insect repellent that contains DEET, picaridin, oil of lemon eucalyptus, or IR 3535 according to label instructions. The CDC does not recommend use of products containing oil of lemon eucalyptus or para-menthane-diol on children under 3. Consult a physician before using repellents on children under 3.
* **REPORT** – report locations where you see water sitting stagnant for more than a week such as roadside ditches, flooded yards, and similar locations that may produce mosquitoes.  The local health department or city government may be able to add larvicide to the water, which will kill any mosquito larvae.

Last year, 67 counties in Illinois reported positive WNV mosquitoes, birds, humans and/or horses.  So far in 2024, there have been 2,113 positive mosquito batches, 29 positive birds, and one positive horse from 57 counties. This year, the first mosquito batches to test positive for WNV were reported May 14 in Cook and Morgan Counties.

[Surveillance for West Nile virus in Illinois](/topics-services/diseases-and-conditions/west-nile-virus/surveillance.html) involves reporting and investigation of individuals with West Nile virus symptoms and clinical laboratory testing. Environmental surveillance includes laboratory testing on mosquito batches, dead birds, as well as testing sick horses. People who observe a sick or dying bird should contact their local health department, which can determine if the bird will be picked up for testing.

Additional information and data on WNV in Illinois can be found at: [**West Nile virus**](/topics-services/diseases-and-conditions/west-nile-virus.html).

### West Nile Virus in Los Angeles County

[**West Nile virus**](https://www.glacvcd.org/west-nile-virus)is the most common mosquito-borne disease that affects residents in Los Angeles County. Public health agencies detect West Nile virus every year in L.A. County which means it's endemic and found naturally in our city environments.

Our agency reports data related to mosquitoes. Human cases are reported by the [L.A. County Department of Public Health](http://publichealth.lacounty.gov/acd/VectorWestNile.htm).

The disease surveillance program serves as an early warning system in the detection of mosquito-borne viruses that can infect people and animals.
